## After this lecture you can

- turn the distributional hypothesis into a matrix, reweight it with PPMI and compress it with truncated SVD
- write skip-gram with negative sampling from scratch and explain it as a logistic regression
- choose between word2vec, GloVe, fastText and doc2vec for a stated problem, and defend it
- diagnose three defects of the space: anisotropy, frequency in the vector, and cosine confusing "mentioned together" with "means the same"
- state precisely what a static embedding cannot do — which is what Ch. 7 exists to fix

::: {.notes}
The chapter's seven learning objectives, condensed to five. In full: explain the
distributional hypothesis and turn it into a matrix, then into coordinates;
reweight co-occurrence counts with PPMI, the score for how much more often two
words land together than chance predicts; compress the result with truncated
SVD, the method that keeps a table's strongest patterns and drops the rest, and
say what each step fixes; write skip-gram with negative sampling from scratch
and explain it as a logistic regression; choose between word2vec, GloVe,
fastText and doc2vec and defend it; diagnose three defects of the space —
vectors sharing a common direction (anisotropy), a vector recording frequency as
much as meaning, and cosine failing to separate "mentioned together" from "means
the same thing"; and state precisely what a static embedding cannot do, which is
exactly what Chapter 7 (Transformers and Attention) exists to fix.

The route: we build the space twice. First by counting, because that version can
be checked by hand and every number is small enough to print. Then by
predicting, which is word2vec — from scratch, gradients included — before
showing that the two routes were the same route all along. After that: what the
space is good at, the defects it hides, and the one thing it cannot do at all.

This is a dense chapter. If it runs over two sessions, the natural break is
after "Where the −log K comes from".
:::

## The problem, in one sentence

- Ch. 2 built document vectors that work — and word vectors that do not
- Every word was a one-hot column: `pump`, `pumps` and `impeller` are three orthogonal directions, as unrelated as `pump` and `Wednesday`
- Cosine between any two distinct words: exactly zero. By construction. Always
- Train on *the pump failed*, test on *the pumps failed*: what the model learned about `pump` sits on a coordinate the test sentence never touches

::: {.takeaway}
The whole fix is one idea: [replace the identity matrix with a learned one]{.hl}. Give every word 100 or 300 numbers, placed so that words used alike sit close. That list is an **embedding**.
:::

::: {.notes}
Chapter 2 (Text as Data) ended in an uncomfortable place. How bad is the one-hot
problem? Bad enough that the model cannot generalise across word forms at all.
The two sentences do share `the` and `failed`, so something transfers — but
everything the model learned about `pump` specifically is filed under a
coordinate the second sentence never touches.

Instead of giving each word its own axis, give it a short list of numbers —
100 of them, or 300 — positioned so that words used in similar ways end up near
each other. Think of it as giving every word a set of map coordinates.

For the statisticians in the room: one-hot encoding is a saturated model with
one parameter per category and no pooling. An embedding is the same model with a
low-rank constraint, which is a form of partial pooling. Words that behave alike
are forced to share parameters, and that sharing *is* the generalisation.
:::

## The distributional hypothesis

::: {.lede}
*"You shall know a word by the company it keeps."* — J.R. Firth, 1957
:::

- Harris (1954) had already made the operational version: meaning can be recovered from the distribution of contexts a word appears in
- Words that fill the same slots — *the ___ failed*, *replaced the ___*, *___ pressure* — mean something similar
- [A bet, not a theorem]{.hl}: extraordinarily good for topical and functional similarity; it fails for antonyms, because *hot* and *cold* keep almost identical company
- It needs no labels. Raw text is the supervision

::: {.takeaway}
That is why embeddings were the first place in NLP where more data reliably beat more cleverness.
:::

::: {.notes}
Firth (1957) was making a point about linguistic method; Zellig Harris (1954)
had already made the operational version of it.

Put concretely: if two words appear in the same slots, then whatever they mean,
they mean something similar.

Is that true? Not quite, and it is worth being clear it is a bet rather than a
theorem. Later in the lecture we watch it fail with real numbers:
`increase`/`decrease` at a cosine of 0.881.

But it has one property that made the entire field possible: it needs no
labels.
:::

## Count first: co-occurrence, PPMI, SVD

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}
### Ten sentences

```python
corpus = [
    "the king rules the castle",
    "the queen rules the castle",
    "the king eats an apple",
    "the queen eats a banana",
    "the royal castle is grand",
    "a banana is sweet fruit",
    "an apple is sweet fruit",
    "the man eats an apple",
    "the woman eats a banana",
    "the king and queen are royal",
]
```
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
### Step 1 · count within ±2 tokens

|          | eats | rules | royal | sweet | the |
|:---------|-----:|------:|------:|------:|----:|
| `king`   | 1    | 1     | 0     | 0     | 4   |
| `queen`  | 1    | 1     | 1     | 0     | 3   |
| `apple`  | 2    | 0     | 0     | 1     | 0   |
| `banana` | 2    | 0     | 0     | 1     | 0   |

- `king` ≈ `queen` and `apple` ≈ `banana`: the hypothesis already working
- The largest number in the `king` row is `the`. [Raw counts measure opportunity, not association.]{.hl}
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
Before word2vec there was a recipe with three steps: count what appears near
what, reweight the counts so common words stop dominating, then factorize. We do
all three by hand — partly because it makes everything later much less
mysterious, and partly because Levy and Goldberg (2014) showed that word2vec is
quietly doing the same thing anyway.

The corpus has 10 sentences and a vocabulary of 19 words.

Step 1: the context of a word is a window around it. Window 2 means two tokens
to the left and two to the right. Slide it over every position and add one to
the cell for every (word, neighbour) pair you see. The rows of this matrix *are*
word vectors — 19-dimensional ones — and unlike one-hots they are not
orthogonal. (The `castle` column is all zeros for these four rows, so it is
left off the slide.)

But they have Chapter 2's disease. Total co-occurrences: `the` 22, `eats` 16,
`is` 11, `queen` 10, `king` 9, `a` 8. The largest number in the `king` row is
`the`, which tells you nothing about kings.
:::

## Step 2 · PMI is observed ÷ expected

$$\mathrm{PMI}(w, c) = \log \frac{P(w, c)}{P(w)\,P(c)}$$

- **Ratio 1**: the words co-occur exactly as chance predicts — no relationship, PMI 0
- **Above 1**: they *attract*, positive. **Below 1**: they *avoid* each other, negative
- The negative side is notoriously unreliable: showing that words co-occur *less* than chance takes far more data
- So clip at zero, and call it [positive PMI]{.hl}:

$$\mathrm{PPMI}(w, c) = \max\!\left(0,\ \log \frac{c_{wc}\, N}{c_{w\ast}\, c_{\ast c}}\right)$$

::: {.notes}
We want to ask: do these two words co-occur more often than chance would
predict? Pointwise mutual information asks exactly that. It measures surprise,
not popularity.

Read the fraction like this: the denominator is how often we would *expect* the
two words to land next to each other if they were placed completely
independently; the numerator is how often they actually do. So PMI is nothing
but the log of observed ÷ expected.

In the PPMI formula, c_wc is how often the pair occurred, c_w* is the row total,
c_*c the column total, and N the grand total of the matrix.

PPMI and IDF are the same instinct applied at different levels. IDF asks how
surprising a word is in a document; PMI asks how surprising a word is next to
another word. Both divide an observed frequency by an expected one and take a
log. The section heading in the chapter calls PPMI "IDF's smarter cousin".
:::

## Work one cell by hand

::: {.lede}
All four numbers come from $C$: pair count $c_{wc}$, row total $c_{w\ast}$, column total $c_{\ast c}$, and $N = 144$ — every (word, neighbour) *pair*, not the 51 tokens.
:::

::: {.roomy}
| pair            | observed | expected                     | ratio | PMI      |
|:----------------|---------:|:-----------------------------|------:|---------:|
| `apple`–`sweet` | 1        | $7 \times 6 / 144 = 0.29$    | 3.43  | **1.23** |
| `king`–`the`    | 4        | $9 \times 22 / 144 = 1.38$   | 2.91  | **1.07** |
:::

- [The pair seen once scores higher than the pair seen four times.]{.hl} `the` is everywhere, so most of those four meetings were expected
- In the PPMI matrix `apple`–`sweet` goes from the smallest non-zero count in its row to its *largest* value, 1.23

::: {.notes}
Where the numbers come from. c_wc = 1: how many times `apple` and `sweet` landed
in each other's window. c_w* = 7: the sum of the `apple` row. `apple` occurs three
times in the corpus, with 2, 3 and 2 neighbours: 2 + 3 + 2 = 7. c_*c = 6: the same
sum down the `sweet` column. N = 144: the sum of every cell. Each token
contributes one pair per neighbour in its window — 4 in the middle of a
sentence, 2 or 3 at the edges — so a five-token sentence yields 14 pairs. Nine
five-token sentences and one six-token sentence (18 pairs): 9 × 14 + 18 = 144.

N is the number of pairs, not tokens, because the denominator of PMI is a
product of probabilities: the thing to divide by is how many pairs were counted.

If the two words were sprinkled independently we would expect 7 × 6 / 144 = 0.29
meetings. We observed 1, which is 3.43 times more. log 3.43 = 1.23.

`king`–`the` occurs four times — four times as often as `apple`–`sweet`. But `the`
has a column total of 22 and `king` a row total of 9, so by chance alone we
expect 1.38. The single meeting between `apple` and `sweet` is not explained by
anything. That reversal is the entire point of the formula.

The chapter's analogy: at a crowded party, someone who talks to everyone tells
you nothing when you see them with the guest of honour. Someone who talks to
only three people all evening, one of them the guest of honour, tells you a
great deal.

PPMI rows for the same cells: `king` has `rules` 0.69 and `the` 1.07; `queen`
has `rules` 0.59, `royal` 1.06, `the` 0.67; `apple` and `banana` each have `eats`
0.94 and `sweet` 1.23. The count for `apple`–`sweet` was small because `sweet`
is rare, and PPMI divides that out.
:::

## Quick check · PPMI {.question}

::: {.ask}
Two words each occur 10 times in a million-token corpus and never co-occur. Why clip their negative PMI instead of keeping it?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Expected co-occurrence under independence is about 0.0002, so observing zero is completely unsurprising — no evidence the words avoid each other
- But $\log 0 = -\infty$, and even smoothed it is a large negative number that dominates the vector
- Negative PMI is sampling noise for exactly the words you have least data about — [which is most of them]{.hl}
- Clipping is a crude but effective admission that we cannot estimate them, and it keeps the matrix sparse
:::

::: {.notes}
Give the room a minute, then reveal (one click).

The side effect worth adding: Levy, Goldberg and Dagan (2015) found that tuned
PPMI is competitive with word2vec on most benchmarks — the gap people attributed
to neural networks was largely a gap in hyperparameter care. We come back to
that paper several times today.
:::

## Step 3 · Truncated SVD keeps what repeats

- The PPMI rows already behave: `king` → `queen` 0.55. But `apple` → `man` 0.79, because of one shared sentence, *the man eats an apple*
- Sparse count vectors are brittle exactly where data is thin. Keep only the $d$ directions with the largest singular values:

$$\mathrm{PPMI} \approx U_d \Sigma_d V_d^\top, \qquad \text{embedding} = U_d \Sigma_d$$

- Here five of nineteen directions hold 65.4% of the sum of squares — not of variance, since PPMI is never centred
- Dropping the faint directions is not a regrettable loss of information: [it is the mechanism]{.hl}

::: {.notes}
Nearest neighbours before factorization, PPMI rows in 19 dimensions: `king` →
queen 0.55, are 0.55, man 0.45, the 0.37; `apple` → man 0.79, fruit 0.52,
banana 0.40, is 0.31. `king` → `queen` is right. `apple` → `man` is not: a single
shared sentence in a ten-sentence corpus is enough to fake an association.

The picture behind the notation. Think of the PPMI matrix as a stack of
transparencies. Each one shows a single recurring pattern — these words tend to
sit near those words — printed at a different darkness. Stack all 19 and you
reproduce the matrix exactly. The singular values are the darknesses, sorted
from boldest to faintest; U says how much each word participates in each
pattern. Truncating to d keeps only the boldest few. The faint ones are where a
coincidence lives: a pattern one sentence created and nothing else confirms.
Forcing 19 columns of evidence through 5 numbers means the model can only afford
to store what repeats. Same bargain as a low bit-rate audio file: when the budget
is tight enough, hiss is the first thing to disappear.

Singular values: 5.75, 4.76, 4.03, 3.71, 3.64, 3.08, 3.03, 2.80. The first two
dimensions hold 36.8% of the sum of squares, the first five 65.4%. These are
shares of the total sum of squares, not variance shares; the two coincide only
after centring.

A production warning. Multiplying by Σ is the textbook choice and, on the
evidence, the wrong default. Levy, Goldberg and Dagan (2015) swept W = U_d Σ_d^p
and found p = 0.5 — often even p = 0 — beating p = 1 by up to fifteen points on
similarity benchmarks. Σ loads the dominant direction most heavily, and that
direction is largely frequency — the anisotropy we measure later as a defect. We
keep p = 1 here because it keeps the arithmetic visible; in production, sweep p.
:::

## What the compression actually did

| word pair          | PPMI rows, 19-D | SVD, 5-D | what happened                                                   |
|:-------------------|----------------:|---------:|:----------------------------------------------------------------|
| `apple` – `banana` | 0.40            | **1.00** | never share a sentence; shared contexts link them, and compression makes the link decisive |
| `king` – `queen`   | 0.55            | **0.90** | already right, and got stronger                                  |
| `apple` – `man`    | 0.79            | **0.85** | the one-sentence accident — *not* deleted, but no longer first  |

::: {.takeaway}
SVD does not break the wrong link; it strengthens the right one enough to overtake it. [The ordering improves; the absolute values do not.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.src}
Deerwester et al. 1990 — latent semantic analysis, more than twenty years before word2vec
:::

::: {.notes}
Look at the third row, because this step is usually described wrongly. SVD does
not delete the `apple`–`man` accident: that cosine rises from 0.79 to 0.85. What
changes is the ranking. Before, `apple`'s nearest neighbour was `man` with
`banana` third; now `banana` is first and `man` third. That is what "preferring
signal over noise" actually looks like.

The number to watch is the first row. `apple` and `banana` never once occur in
the same sentence, so nothing links them directly. What links them is that they
keep the same company — both follow `eats`, both precede `is sweet fruit`. The raw
PPMI rows already register that as 0.40, because shared contexts are shared
coordinates; the compression strengthens it to 1.00, enough to reorder the
neighbour list. Call this shared-context generalisation rather than transitivity
— cosine is not a transitive relation — and note that low-rank compression makes
it decisive rather than visible.

Other neighbours after SVD to 5 dimensions: `king` → queen 0.90, are 0.88;
`eats` → an 0.95, a 0.95; `castle` → are 0.82, is 0.80.

This is latent semantic analysis (Deerwester et al. 1990).
:::
