The warning box in the chapter: a dimension that all words share the sign of
cannot separate any of them — it is a common direction, not a contrastive one.
Plotting dimensions 1 and 2 would waste half the picture.

Read the compression printout with that in mind: in two dimensions `king` vs
`queen` has a cosine of 0.996 and `king` vs `banana` 0.141. In a space where
every word shares the sign of the first coordinate, a high cosine is partly the
shared direction talking, not the similarity. And any two one-hots: cosine 0.00,
always.
:::

## From counting to predicting

- Why abandon counting? Not accuracy. The matrix is vocabulary × vocabulary: ten billion *possible* cells at 100,000 words — one monolithic artifact to build before you can factorize
- word2vec (Mikolov et al. 2013): never build the matrix. Train a classifier to *predict* context, then throw the classifier away and keep its weights
- A shallow network: one-hot input → hidden layer = the row of $\mathbf{W}$ for that word, a lookup with no activation → output $\mathbf{W}'$ scores candidate words
- When training ends, $\mathbf{W}'$ is discarded and $\mathbf{W}$ kept: one row per word

::: {.takeaway}
[The product is not the network you train; it is the weights of its first layer.]{.hl} The embedding table at the bottom of a transformer (Ch. 7) is literally the same object.
:::

::: {.notes}
So counting works: royalty landed on one side and food on the other. Why did the
field move on? One reason, and it is not accuracy. Sparse storage keeps only
the non-zeros, but the co-occurrence matrix is still one monolithic artifact you
have to build before you can factorize anything. The alternative is to never
build it, and learn the vectors by asking the model to predict.

The three layers. The input layer is a one-hot vector as long as the
vocabulary. The hidden layer multiplies it by W, and multiplying a one-hot by a
matrix does nothing except pull out that word's row — so the hidden layer is
really a lookup table, often called a projection layer. It is called shallow
because there is only one hidden layer and it carries no activation function.
The output layer is a second matrix, W′, which scores the hidden vector against
candidate words.

The model was a pretext; the weights were the point. 300 numbers per row in the
usual setting.

Two matrices are learned: v for words as centres, u for words as contexts.
Almost everyone keeps v and discards u. Adding them sometimes helps a little;
GloVe's authors recommend it (Pennington et al. 2014).
:::

## CBOW and skip-gram: arrows reversed

::: {.lede}
One window of *the pump failed during the night shift*: centre `failed`, width 2.
:::

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
### CBOW · context → centre

[the]{.chip} [pump]{.chip} [during]{.chip} [the]{.chip} → average → `failed`

- One training example per window
- Faster; the average blurs rare words
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Skip-gram · centre → context

`failed` → its own vector → [the]{.chip} [pump]{.chip} [during]{.chip} [the]{.chip}

- Four training examples per window
- Slower; much better on rare words
:::

::::

::: {.takeaway}
Both learn $\mathbf{W}$ (word → vector) and $\mathbf{W}'$ (scores partners), and both throw $\mathbf{W}'$ away. [Skip-gram is the variant that won]{.hl}; the rest of the chapter uses it.
:::

::: {.notes}
A static version of the chapter's two-architecture figure. CBOW averages the
surrounding words and predicts the centre. Skip-gram takes the centre word and
predicts each surrounding word in turn.

Slide a window over the corpus and every position yields training examples. For
skip-gram with centre `failed`, the pairs are (failed, the), (failed, pump),
(failed, during), (failed, the). The book's interactive version lets students
type a sentence and move the centre and window.

This is the entire supervision signal. No labels, no annotation — just the text,
cut into pairs. A corpus of 6 billion tokens with window 5 yields about 60
billion of these.

The vectors you download are the rows of W.
:::

## Negative sampling is a logistic regression {.smaller}

- A softmax over a 400,000-word vocabulary, for every one of billions of pairs, is hopeless
- Ask instead: [is this a *real* pair from the corpus, or one I made up?]{.hl} For each real pair, draw $K$ fakes from a noise distribution and label them 0

$$P(\text{real} \mid w, c) = \sigma(\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c), \qquad \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}$$

$$\mathcal{L} = -\log \sigma(\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c) - \sum_{k=1}^{K} \log \sigma(-\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_{n_k})$$

- One term pulls together, $K$ terms push apart. Nothing else is happening
- With $K = 5$: six dot products per pair instead of 400,000, no normalisation — roughly 67,000 times cheaper

::: {.src}
Mikolov et al. 2013
:::

::: {.notes}
There is one problem left, and it is a bad one. To turn a score into a
probability you normalise over the whole vocabulary, for every training pair.
That is not a training run anybody finishes.

The fix is almost embarrassingly simple, and it is the reason word2vec was
practical: replace it with a question a statistician recognises instantly. That
is binary classification — a logistic regression whose linear predictor is the
dot product of the two words' vectors — minimising the usual log loss.

Read the loss in two halves. The first term is small when σ(v·u) is close to 1,
so it pays you for giving real pairs a large dot product. The second is small
when the dot product with each fake partner is very negative.

The chapter's figure: the full softmax asks "which of 400,000 words comes next?"
— one question with 400,000 answers. Negative sampling asks "is this pair
real?" six times — six questions with two answers each (the true partner `pump`,
fakes such as `opera`, `zinc`, `tariff`, `carbon`, `helix`).

The book's loss widget: training pushes the dot product of real pairs to the
right and fake pairs to the left. Since the dot product of two unit-length
vectors is their cosine, "similar words have similar vectors" is not an emergent
property — it is literally the loss function.

"Shallow neural network" and "logistic regression" are not competing
explanations: a single linear layer with no activation, followed by a sigmoid
and a log loss, is by definition a logistic regression. Reach for the first to
describe the architecture, the second to compute the gradient. If you have ever
fitted a logistic regression, you have fitted 99% of word2vec. The only unusual
part is that both the predictors and the coefficients are learned, which makes it
a factorization rather than a regression.
:::

## Work one update by hand

::: {.lede}
Four dimensions instead of 300. Centre `failed`: $\mathbf{v} = (0.4,\ -0.2,\ 0.7,\ 0.1)$. True partner `pump`: $\mathbf{u} = (0.5,\ 0.1,\ 0.6,\ -0.3)$. Sampled fake `opera`: $\mathbf{u} = (-0.3,\ 0.6,\ -0.2,\ 0.4)$.
:::

::: {.roomy}
| pair             | $y$ | $\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{u}$ | $\sigma(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{u})$ | loss  | $\sigma - y$ |
|:-----------------|----:|------------------------------:|--------------------------------------:|------:|-------------:|
| `failed`–`pump`  | 1   | 0.57                          | 0.639                                 | 0.448 | −0.361       |
| `failed`–`opera` | 0   | −0.34                         | 0.416                                 | 0.538 | 0.416        |
:::

- The derivative of the loss with respect to the dot product is $\sigma(\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{u}) - y$: [prediction minus target]{.hl}, as in every logistic regression
- Update only $\mathbf{v}$ at learning rate 0.05: `failed`·`pump` 0.570 → **0.590**; `failed`·`opera` −0.340 → −0.359
- Update the context vectors too: 0.603 and −0.374 — same directions, about 1.6 times as far

::: {.notes}
For the real pair: (0.4)(0.5) + (−0.2)(0.1) + (0.7)(0.6) + (0.1)(−0.3) = 0.57, so
σ(0.57) = 0.639 — the model currently gives this pair a 64% chance of being
genuine — and its loss contribution is −log 0.639 = 0.448.

For the fake pair the dot product is −0.34, giving σ(0.34) = 0.584 for "fake"
and a loss of −log 0.584 = 0.538. The model is already leaning the right way on
both, but not confidently, so both get nudged.

For `pump`, 0.639 − 1 = −0.361: negative, so the dot product goes up. For `opera`,
0.416 − 0 = 0.416: positive, so the dot product goes down.

Holding the context vectors fixed, the gradient for v is the sum of both terms:
(0.639 − 1)·u_pump + (0.416 − 0)·u_opera = (−0.305, 0.213, −0.300, 0.275). That
is what `gv` in the training code computes in one einsum.

These are tiny movements. Multiply them by tens of billions of pairs and you get
the geometry that made these models famous: no cleverness, just an enormous
number of very small corrections.
:::

## Only seven rows move

$$\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{v}_w} = \bigl(\sigma(z) - y\bigr)\,\mathbf{u}_c, \qquad \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \mathbf{u}_c} = \bigl(\sigma(z) - y\bigr)\,\mathbf{v}_w$$

- Each vector is dragged along the other, by how wrong the prediction was. A pair already scored correctly barely moves
- One pair with $K = 5$: one row of $\mathbf{W}$, plus $1 + K$ rows of $\mathbf{W}'$ — **seven rows**
- Every other row entered no dot product, so its gradient is [exactly zero]{.hl} — not small
- Our from-scratch model has 37,354 rows; seven is **0.019%**. A full softmax touches 18,678 per pair: **2,668 times** the arithmetic

::: {.notes}
The derivation, for students who want to see it fall out. Write z = v·u. The
sigmoid has a tidy derivative, σ′(z) = σ(z)(1 − σ(z)). Differentiate −log σ(z)
with the chain rule: −σ′(z)/σ(z) = σ(z) − 1. The σ(z) cancels, which is the
whole reason log loss is paired with the sigmoid rather than, say, squared
error. For a negative sample the term is −log σ(−z) and the same two lines give
σ(z). Both collapse into σ(z) − y. One more chain-rule step, since ∂z/∂v = u,
gives the two gradients on the slide.

A pair the model already scores correctly produces a near-zero gradient; the
learning concentrates on pairs it gets wrong. That self-limiting behaviour is
why the method survives billions of updates without diverging.

The count: the model we train from scratch has a vocabulary of 18,677, 100
dimensions, two matrices — 37,354 rows and 3,735,400 parameters. One pair touches
7 rows. That is why billions of updates finish in hours on one machine. With a
full softmax the denominator sums over every word, so every output vector gets a
non-zero gradient: 18,678 rows, half of all rows, for every pair.

Practical consequence: the gradient of an embedding matrix is sparse. PyTorch's
`nn.Embedding(..., sparse=True)` and the `SparseAdam` optimizer come straight out
of this fact. And a word learns only as much as it occurs or gets drawn as a
negative — another way to read why the 0.75 exponent on the next slide matters.
:::

## Two details that matter more than the architecture

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%"}
### Subsampling frequent words

| share of corpus  | example        | kept | discarded |
|:-----------------|:---------------|-----:|----------:|
| 5%               | `the`          | 0.16 | 84%       |
| 1%               | `of`, `and`    | 0.42 | 58%       |
| 0.1% ($= t$)     | mid-frequency  | 1.00 | 0%        |
| 0.01% and below  | the tail       | 1.00 | 0%        |

In our run: 26.6% of in-vocabulary tokens go, 6,397,826 → 4,698,743.
:::

::: {.column width="48%" .compact}
### Negatives drawn from $f(w)^{0.75}$

- A word 5,000 times more frequent is only about 595 times more likely to be drawn — the gap narrows about eightfold
- A word learns only from being *contrasted*; the exponent buys the tail a share of the signal
- Chosen empirically: 0.75 has no derivation
:::

::::

::: {.takeaway}
Levy et al. (2015) identified the exponent as one of the hyperparameters [doing much of the work people credited to the model]{.hl}.
:::

::: {.notes}
Subsampling. `the` appears next to everything, so pairs containing it carry
almost no information but make up a huge share of the data. word2vec keeps word w
with probability min(1, (sqrt(f/t) + 1) · t/f), t ≈ 10⁻³. Any word below a
thousandth of the corpus is always kept. This is the formula in word2vec's C
source, which every implementation follows; the published paper states a
different one, P(discard) = 1 − sqrt(t/f). The code is what was actually run — a
small reminder to read the implementation, not only the paper.

So this is not a gentle reweighting: it deletes five out of every six
occurrences of `the`, and leaves the tail alone. Almost all of what it throws away
in the run is `the`, `of`, `and` and their friends. (6,397,826 is what is left of
6,794,527 tokens read once everything below min_count = 20 is dropped.)

A second benefit: deleting a token widens the windows around it. With `the`
removed, the words either side become neighbours — subsampling creates
informative pairs, not only removes uninformative ones.

The exponent. Raising probabilities to a power below 1 pulls the smallest ones
up furthest in relative terms: 0.5^0.75 is 19% larger than 0.5, while
0.001^0.75 is 5.6 times larger than 0.001. Renormalising moves mass from the
head to the tail. 5000^0.75 ≈ 595. A word never drawn as a negative is never
pushed away from anything, and its vector simply drifts.

Levy, Goldberg and Dagan (2015) identify the exponent as one of the
hyperparameters doing much of the work people were crediting to the model.
:::

## Writing it from scratch

::: {.lede}
About sixty lines of NumPy, no framework, trained on the first 40 million characters of `text8`. The heart of it:
:::

```python
v = Wc[c]                                              # (B, D)
u = Wo[targets]                                        # (B, K+1, D)
score = sigmoid(np.einsum("bkd,bd->bk", u, v))         # (B, K+1)
err = (score - labels).astype(np.float32)              # the residual
gv = np.einsum("bk,bkd->bd", err, u)
gu = err[:, :, None] * v[:, None, :]
np.clip(gv, -1.0, 1.0, out=gv)
np.clip(gu, -1.0, 1.0, out=gu)
np.add.at(Wc, c, -lr * gv)
np.add.at(Wo, targets.ravel(), (-lr * gu).reshape(-1, D))
```

::: {.takeaway}
`err = score - labels` is predicted minus observed — [the residual of a logistic regression]{.hl}. After three epochs: `monday` → friday 0.87, `france` → spain 0.79, `physics` → mechanics 0.82.
:::

::: {.notes}
The full listing is in the chapter: vocabulary with min_count 20 (18,677 words),
subsampling, the 0.75 noise distribution, D = 100, K = 5, window 5, 3 epochs,
learning rate 0.02, batches of 2,048. Every gradient below `err` is that residual
times the other vector.

Run: 6,794,527 tokens read; 4,698,743 after subsampling; 46,987,400 training
pairs; loss 4.159 → 2.351; trained in 1,865 s. Other neighbours: `king` → consort
0.75, kings 0.75; `three` → four 0.95; `car` → racing 0.74, cars 0.74.

Two simplifications stated in the code: the window is fixed at 5, whereas
word2vec samples an effective width from 1 to 5; and pairs cross document
boundaries, harmless on text8, wrong on separate documents. Batches are drawn
with replacement, so "3 epochs" is not comparable with gensim's epochs = 3.

The chapter's intuition check — why does `np.add.at` need gradient clipping?
Real word2vec updates one pair at a time. Batching breaks that: `np.add.at`
accumulates every gradient for a repeated index and applies the sum in one step;
a common word can appear a hundred times in a batch of 2,048. Without clipping
this run diverged to nan within half an epoch — which is what happened the first
time it was run for the chapter, at learning rate 0.05. Be precise: the clip
bounds each per-example contribution, not the accumulated row update; what it
prevents is one large residual multiplied by a context vector whose norm has
grown. The clean fix divides each row's accumulated gradient by its count in the
batch. It is the price of vectorising a sequential algorithm — and a good example
of why "I reimplemented the paper and it didn't work" is usually about
optimisation details rather than the equations.
:::

## Two routes, one destination

::: {.lede}
Levy & Goldberg (2014): skip-gram with negative sampling *implicitly factorizes* a matrix.
:::

$$\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c = \mathrm{PMI}(w, c) - \log K$$

- This holds at the optimum, with the dot products free. Nobody builds that matrix: [it is never constructed, it is *reached*]{.hl}
- PMI, not PPMI: a never-seen pair is $-\infty$. The explicit matrix you would build is SPPMI $= \max(\mathrm{PMI} - \log K,\ 0)$

::: {.takeaway}
Levy et al. (2015): give count methods the hyperparameters word2vec quietly uses, and the performance gap mostly disappears.
:::

::: {.src}
Baroni et al. 2014 · Levy & Goldberg 2014 · Levy, Goldberg & Dagan 2015
:::

::: {.notes}
For a year the field treated counting (LSA, PPMI+SVD) and predicting (word2vec)
as rival philosophies. Baroni, Dinu and Kruszewski (2014) framed it as a contest
and reported predicting winning. Then Levy and Goldberg proved the implicit
factorization. The neural network was a matrix factorization wearing a costume.

The algorithm only ever sees one pair at a time and nudges two vectors. Yet run
it to convergence and read off the dot product for any pair, and you get that
pair's PMI minus a constant.

The clipping lives in a different place from route A: it is a patch applied
when you construct an explicit SPPMI matrix. Training SGNS clips nothing — it
never has to represent −∞, because it only sees the pairs it samples.

The −log K term: raising K contrasts each real pair against more fakes, which
lowers the target for every dot product by the same fixed amount — uniform in the
implicit matrix, which is not the same as shifting every word vector by an
offset. In practice K is one of the less important settings, an empirical
observation rather than a consequence of the algebra.

The follow-up hyperparameters: subsampling, context distribution smoothing,
dynamic windows. The lesson generalises: when a new method beats an old one, some
of the improvement is the method and some is the tuning, and the split is rarely
reported.
:::

## Where the −log K comes from

::: {.lede}
Fix one pair; treat $z = \mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c$ as a free number. Its real count pulls up, and the sampler's accidental draws — $K$ times the chance of drawing $c$ — push down:
:::

$$P(w,c)\,\log \sigma(z) \;+\; K\,P(w)P(c)\,\log \sigma(-z)$$

Set the derivative to zero, $P(w,c)\bigl(1 - \sigma(z)\bigr) = K\,P(w)P(c)\,\sigma(z)$, and solve:

$$z = \log \frac{P(w,c)}{K\,P(w)P(c)} = \mathrm{PMI}(w,c) - \log K$$

::: {.small-note}
The theorem fixes the *target*, not the compromise. At low rank, SVD minimises squared error weighting every cell equally; SGNS minimises a logistic loss weighted by how often each pair was sampled. Same target, different losses — not generally the same vectors.
:::

::: {.notes}
Derivatives used: d/dz log σ(z) = 1 − σ(z) and d/dz log σ(−z) = −σ(z). After
solving for σ(z), convert back through z = log(σ/(1 − σ)).

The one assumption doing real work is that z can be chosen freely for every
pair. It cannot: the dot products share the same vectors, and with d far below
the vocabulary size the model must compromise.

A second assumption hides in the notation and contradicts the code: writing the
noise weight as K·P(w)P(c) assumes raw unigram negatives. word2vec draws from
f(c)^0.75 instead, which gives PMI against a smoothed context distribution.
Levy, Goldberg and Dagan (2015) call this context distribution smoothing and
show it transfers to PPMI+SVD, where it is worth several points. So the 0.75
exponent changes which matrix the algorithm factorizes.

The statistical difference, for the statisticians. Truncated SVD gives the best
rank-d approximation in Frobenius norm (Eckart–Young–Mirsky), weighting every
cell equally — and most cells of a PPMI matrix are zero. SVD spends most of its
budget faithfully reproducing "these two words never met". SGNS never sees a
cell it did not sample. That, and not the neural framing, is where SGNS's
advantage on rare words comes from — and it is exactly the defect GloVe's
weighting function was designed to fix. Read the three methods as three answers
to one question: how much should a cell you barely observed count?

If the lecture is split in two, this is the place.
:::

## GloVe: counting, with a loss function

$$\mathcal{L} = \sum_{w,c} f(X_{wc}) \left(\mathbf{v}_w \cdot \mathbf{u}_c + b_w + b_c - \log X_{wc}\right)^2$$

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="58%" .compact}
- Weighted least squares on log counts, one bias per word — about as classical as statistics gets
- **Why $\log X$?** Counts are Zipfian; logs turn ratios into differences
- **Why biases?** They absorb row and column totals: [GloVe rediscovers PMI, but fits it]{.hl}
- **Why $f$?** $f(0) = 0$, so $\log 0$ is never evaluated; the cap stops the most frequent pairs dominating
:::

::: {.column width="42%"}
$f(x) = (x/x_{\max})^{3/4}$ below $x_{\max} = 100$, else 1

| $X_{wc}$ | $f(X_{wc})$ |
|--------:|------------:|
| 0       | 0.00        |
| 1       | 0.03        |
| 10      | 0.18        |
| 100     | 1.00        |
| 100,000 | 1.00        |
:::

::::

::: {.src}
Pennington et al. 2014
:::

::: {.notes}
If counting and predicting are the same thing underneath: could you do the
counting explicitly and still get the benefits of gradient descent? GloVe took
that synthesis seriously. Build the global co-occurrence matrix, then fit vectors
so that dot products reproduce log co-occurrence counts, weighting rare pairs
down.

Why log X: a few pairs occur millions of times, most once. Fitting raw counts
would make the loss entirely about `of the`.

Why biases: b_w absorbs anything that depends only on w, b_c anything that
depends only on c — exactly the row and column totals. So v·u is left to explain
what is left over after each word's overall frequency. Dividing by the row and
column totals in the PMI formula is subtracting their logs, and that is what
these biases learn to do.

Why f: a pair that never co-occurs has log 0 = −∞, and a pair that co-occurs
constantly would swamp everything. f(0) = 0 means the infinity's coefficient is
zero. The cap: a pair seen 100,000 times gets the same weight as one seen 100
times, so the most frequent — and least informative — pairs cannot dominate. The
same instinct as word2vec's subsampling, implemented as a weight rather than a
deletion. The exponent is even the same 0.75.
:::

## What a word is now

::: {.lede}
Pretrained GloVe: 400,000 vectors, 100 dimensions, trained on Wikipedia 2014 + Gigaword 5 (6 billion tokens).
:::

| query    | nearest neighbours                                  | what it shows                          |
|:---------|:----------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------|
| `king`   | prince 0.77, queen 0.75, son 0.70                   | —                                      |
| `pump`   | pumps 0.84, pumping 0.77, pumped 0.71               | `pumps` is a neighbour, not an orthogonal axis |
| `turkey` | ankara 0.75, turkish 0.72, greece 0.71              | the country — no trace of the bird     |
| `python` | monty 0.69, php 0.59, perl 0.58, flipper 0.51       | three meanings blended into one point  |
| `bank`   | banks 0.81, banking 0.75, credit 0.70               | the river bank has been outvoted       |

::: {.takeaway}
The defining limitation of a static embedding: [one vector per word form, whatever the context]{.hl}. Fixing it is the biggest motivation for the contextual models of Ch. 7.
:::

::: {.notes}
We use the pretrained GloVe vectors for the rest of the chapter, because they
are what most people reach for when they want static embeddings.

`king` starts −0.323, −0.876, 0.22, 0.253, … and has norm 6.118. One hundred
numbers, none of which means anything on its own. The dimensions are not
"royalty" and "gender" — they are an arbitrary basis of a learned space. Asking
what dimension 37 means is like asking what one principal component of a
multivariate dataset means on its own: sometimes there is an answer; usually
there is not.

`python` returns `monty` and `cleese` (the comedy troupe), `php` and `perl` (the
language), and `flipper` (the animal).

A Turkish example from the English chapter: *yüz* means face, it means hundred,
and it is the imperative "swim". A static model gives it one row, the weighted
average of all three — a location that means none of them. Ask that vector
whether a review mentioning *yüz* is about a face cream or a hundred-lira price
and it cannot answer: the answer depends on the sentence, and the vector was
fixed before the sentence existed. No amount of training data changes that.
:::

## king − man + woman ≈ queen?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
### What `gensim` returns

::: {.roomy}
| word     | cosine |
|:---------|-------:|
| queen    | 0.7699 |
| monarch  | 0.6843 |
| throne   | 0.6756 |
| daughter | 0.6595 |
| princess | 0.6521 |
:::
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### The same query, unfiltered

::: {.roomy}
| word      | cosine |
|:----------|-------:|
| **king**  | 0.8552 |
| queen     | 0.7834 |
| monarch   | 0.6934 |
| throne    | 0.6833 |
| daughter  | 0.6809 |
:::
:::

::::

::: {.takeaway}
`gensim` silently excludes the three input words. [The nearest vector is `king`, by a wide margin]{.hl} — the famous result depends on a post-hoc filter.
:::

::: {.notes}
The result that made embeddings famous outside NLP. It is genuinely striking:
nobody told the model about gender, yet the offset between `man` and `woman` is
roughly the offset between `king` and `queen`.

Why subtraction should mean anything: a difference of two vectors is a
direction of travel. king − man is "whatever you have to change about `man` to
arrive at `king`". Following that from `woman` lands on `queen` only if the
instruction is the same in both places — only if the four words form a
parallelogram. And there is a reason they might: `man` and `woman` appear in
near-identical contexts apart from the words that mark gender, so their vectors
differ mostly along the direction those contexts push. The same holds for `king`
and `queen`. If gender is one consistent direction, the offsets coincide.

That "if" is doing a lot of work.

Subtracting `man` and adding `woman` moved the vector, but not far enough to
leave `king`'s neighbourhood. This is not a gotcha — the filter is defensible,
since you rarely want an input echoed back — but it changes what the
demonstration proves.
:::

## What the analogy hides

- The filtered method is **3CosAdd**; **3CosMul** (Levy & Goldberg 2014) replaces the sum of cosines with a ratio and gains a few points
- Linzen (2016): return the nearest neighbour of `woman`, never look at `king` or `man` — that alone recovers a large share of the reported accuracy
- In five of the book's eight example analogies, the raw nearest neighbour is an input word
- `mice − mouse + goose`: `geese` is only rank 5, behind `cows` and `rats`
- `madrid − spain + germany` → `munich`, not `berlin`: [the model learned "German city", not "capital of"]{.hl}

::: {.notes}
The headline analogy number measures neighbourhood structure at least as much as
it measures a relation — that is Linzen's point. Nissim, van Noord and van der
Goot (2020) make the complementary point about how such results get presented.

The eight analogies in the book's explorer (real GloVe results, with and without
the filter): king − man + woman, paris − france + italy, walking − walk + swim,
bigger − big + small, madrid − spain + germany, windows − microsoft + google,
mice − mouse + goose, einstein − physics + biology. Raw top hits:
`walking − walk + swim` → swim 0.855; `windows − microsoft + google` → windows 0.845;
`einstein − physics + biology` → einstein 0.738. `paris − france + italy` gives
rome 0.808 cleanly.

The chapter also projects thirty words to two dimensions: royalty, people,
countries, capitals and verb forms separate cleanly, countries near their
capitals. Read it with care: those are the first two principal components of
those thirty vectors, not of all 400,000 — part of why the groups look so clean —
and they keep only 37.5% of the variance. Every number in the chapter is computed
in 100 dimensions, never from a projection.
:::

## Turkish makes more than twice the word forms

::: {.lede}
Two Wikipedia samples of comparable size:
:::

|                                        | Turkish   | English   |
|:---------------------------------------|----------:|----------:|
| tokens                                 | 1,458,213 | 1,828,840 |
| distinct word forms                    | 138,578   | 78,140    |
| forms seen after 1 million tokens      | 112,644   | 52,347    |
| forms seen exactly once (hapax)        | 50.0%     | 46.7%     |
| held-out tokens never seen in training | 7.33%     | 4.72%     |

::: {.takeaway}
`ev`, `evim`, `evimde`, `evimdeki`, `evlerimizdekiler` are five vocabulary entries. [Nearly one Turkish token in fourteen in held-out text is unseen, and half the vectors come from a single observation.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
Everything so far has one vector per word form, learned only for forms seen in
training. Ask for a word the model never saw — an out-of-vocabulary word — and
you get an exception. For English that is an annoyance. For Turkish it is a
design failure.

Turkish produced 138,578 distinct forms from 1.46 million tokens; English
produced 78,140 from more tokens, 1.83 million. Each Turkish form needs its own
vector, estimated from its own sparse handful of occurrences.

Vocabulary growth, new forms per million tokens: Turkish 45,688 at 250k, 73,435
at 500k, 97,412 at 750k, 112,644 at 1M, 126,389 at 1.25M; English 22,869,
34,016, 42,854, 52,347, 60,178. More than twice as many, and the curve is not
flattening.

Hapax: Turkish 69,296 of 138,578 types; English 36,503 of 78,140.
Out-of-vocabulary rate, training on 90% and testing on the last 10%: Turkish
7.33% of tokens and 28.99% of types unseen; English 4.72% and 23.29%.
:::

## fastText: a word is the sum of its pieces

$$\mathbf{v}_{\text{word}} = \mathbf{v}_{\langle\text{word}\rangle} + \sum_{n\text{-grams } g} \mathbf{v}_g$$

- Every n-gram vector is trained by *every* word containing it: `<pu` by `pump`, `pumps`, `pumped`, `pumping`, `punch` …
- A rare word is assembled from pieces that each had plentiful data; an unseen word still has n-grams — [the vocabulary becomes open]{.hl}

**pumps**, seen in training: [**&lt;pu**]{.chip} [**pum**]{.chip} [**ump**]{.chip} [mps]{.chip} [ps&gt;]{.chip} [&lt;pumps&gt;]{.chip}

**pumpage**, never seen: [**&lt;pu**]{.chip} [**pum**]{.chip} [**ump**]{.chip} [mpa]{.chip} [pag]{.chip} [age]{.chip} [ge&gt;]{.chip} — word2vec: `KeyError`

::: {.small-note}
Drawn with 3-grams; fastText's default is every n-gram of length 3 to 6, so a real `pumpage` decomposes into 22 pieces, not 7.
:::

::: {.notes}
fastText's answer (Bojanowski et al. 2017) is to stop treating a word as atomic:
represent it as the sum of its character n-grams — its subwords — plus a vector
for the whole word.

The bold pieces are shared. That overlap is the whole trick: an unseen word
inherits meaning from the words it is spelled like. `pumpage` has no whole-word
vector, so the n-grams carry it alone.

The angle brackets mark word boundaries; that is how the model distinguishes a
suffix from the same letters mid-word. The book's widget lets students type a
word — the default is `kitaplarımızdaki` against `kitaplar` — and see which
n-grams are shared.

The trade is visible in the equation. A word's identity is spread across its
spelling, so fastText cannot easily represent a word whose meaning has nothing
to do with how it is written. Sums are commutative and indifferent; they cannot
tell `<pu` that it means something different inside `punch` than inside `pump`.
:::

## What subwords buy

::: {.lede}
Out-of-vocabulary words: two Turkish forms the Turkish Wikipedia sample never contained, then two typos. word2vec raises `KeyError`; fastText still answers:
:::

| word               | fastText's nearest neighbours                            |
|:-------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------|
| `kitaplarımızdaki` | kitapları 0.91, kitapların 0.91, kitaplıkları 0.90       |
| `bilgisayarcılık`  | bilgisayara 0.96, bilgisayarlı 0.96, bilgisayar 0.96     |
| `philosphy`        | philosophy 0.96, philosophie 0.95, philosophies 0.94     |
| `governmentt`      | government 0.98, governments 0.94, governmental 0.93     |

::: {.takeaway}
The same trick handles typos — [why fastText is a quietly popular choice for user-generated text]{.hl}.
:::

::: {.notes}
The two Turkish rows come from word2vec and fastText trained on the same Turkish
Wikipedia sample: neither word is in either model's vocabulary, and word2vec
raises KeyError on both. The last two rows are typos, not in the vocabulary
either.

Fourth neighbours, for completeness: `kitaplarımızdaki` → kitaplarda 0.90;
`bilgisayarcılık` → bilgisayarı 0.96; `philosphy` → philology 0.94;
`governmentt` → governs 0.91.
:::

## What subwords cost

| query                          | fastText                            | word2vec                                    |
|:-------------------------------|:------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------|
| `kitap` (book)                 | kitapta 0.96, kitaba 0.95, kitab 0.94 | eseri 0.81, makale 0.80, eseriyle 0.80    |
| `yaz` (summer; also "write")   | yao 0.78, yağ 0.77, yağdı 0.77      | kış 0.86, olimpiyatları 0.84, aylarında 0.83 |
| cosine `kitap`–`kitle`         | +0.667                              | +0.446                                      |

- `kitap`: inflections versus *semantic* neighbours. Which you want depends entirely on the task
- `yaz`: three-character words are mostly n-gram, so the subword signal drowns the semantic one

::: {.takeaway}
Subwords trade semantic precision for morphological coverage. [Take the trade when the vocabulary is open and words are long; refuse it when short words carry the load.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
Now the part the tutorials skip. Character n-grams buy morphology by assuming
similar spelling implies similar meaning — and in any language that assumption is
sometimes badly wrong.

`kitap`: word2vec returns `eseri` (his/her work) and `makale` (article).

`yaz`: word2vec has learned the season — `kış` (winter), `olimpiyatları`
(olympics), `gündönümü` (solstice). fastText returns `yao`, `yağ` (oil), `yayoi`,
`yay` (bow): words that share letters and nothing else.

`kitap` (book) and `kitle` (mass, crowd) are unrelated words that share three
letters; fastText scores them half again as similar as word2vec does.

The rule in full: take the trade when your vocabulary is open and your words are
long — Turkish, Finnish, Hungarian, German compounds, chemical names, product
codes, user-generated text. Refuse it when the vocabulary is closed and short
words carry the load. This is the same trade-off as BPE in Chapter 2, now applied
to meaning rather than to tokenization.
:::

## Documents as vectors

::: {.lede}
Chapter 2's four 20 Newsgroups categories, same split, same logistic regression on top:
:::

| representation                   | accuracy | dimensions |
|:---------------------------------|---------:|-----------:|
| TF-IDF (Ch. 2 baseline)          | **0.853** | 32,014    |
| averaged GloVe                   | 0.820    | 100        |
| idf-weighted averaged GloVe      | 0.822    | 100        |
| doc2vec (PV-DBOW, 40 epochs)     | 0.839    | 100        |
| averaged GloVe + doc2vec         | 0.845    | 200        |

::: {.takeaway}
[The sparse Ch. 2 baseline wins.]{.hl} Dense vectors buy size, not accuracy: 0.820 against 0.853 with 320 times fewer dimensions.
:::

::: {.small-note}
Test set ≈ 1,500 documents, so SE ≈ 0.010: the 1.9-point doc2vec gap is about two SEs on one split, the 0.2-point gap is noise, the 3.3-point TF-IDF gap survives.
:::

::: {.notes}
The obvious move is to average the word vectors in a document: a 100-dimensional
document vector instead of a 32,000-dimensional sparse one. doc2vec (Le and
Mikolov 2014) is less naive: it learns a vector per document by the same
negative-sampling trick, treating the document id as an extra context. Two
flavours, the CBOW and skip-gram of the document world: PV-DM adds a document
slot to CBOW; PV-DBOW uses the document vector alone to predict words drawn from
it. Le and Mikolov recommend PV-DM; Lau and Baldwin (2016) re-ran both carefully
and found PV-DBOW at least as strong and much cheaper, which is why gensim's
defaults follow it. doc2vec is also the field's best-known reproducibility case:
the paper's headline IMDB error rate was not independently reproduced for years,
and the gap turned out to be hyperparameters and training length.

The catch at inference: a new document has no row, so its vector needs more
gradient steps — which is why averaging, for all its flaws, is still the more
common choice.

On the statistics: the right test for the small gaps is McNemar's on the paired
predictions, and the right presentation a mean over several splits with a
spread.

If you are storing ten million document vectors, or doing nearest-neighbour
search over them, the dimension ratio decides your architecture. If you are
classifying four newsgroups on 2,327 training documents, it buys nothing.

Why does averaging do so well at all? Topic classification is largely a
bag-of-topics problem, and the average of a document's word vectors is a decent
estimate of its topic centroid. Arora, Liang and Ma (2017) show a weighted average
plus removal of the first principal component is a hard baseline to beat for
sentence similarity.
:::

## What averaging destroys

- Coverage: GloVe knows 98.6% of the corpus's *tokens* but only 84.5% of its *types* — the missing 15% are the rare, informative, domain-specific words, and averaging silently drops them

```text
a = "the pump failed and the valve is fine"
b = "the valve failed and the pump is fine"
```

::: {.fragment}
- Cosine of the two averaged vectors: **1.0000**. Not similar — [identical]{.hl}, because addition is commutative
- Two sentences that would send a maintenance crew to opposite ends of the plant share one vector
:::

::: {.takeaway}
Chapter 2's bag-of-words problem, still unsolved, now in 100 dimensions instead of 32,000. Word order needs a model that reads the sequence (Ch. 6, Ch. 7).
:::

::: {.notes}
Ask the room for the cosine before revealing (one click).

Coverage in numbers: 23,395 of 27,681 types.

The code in the chapter averages the GloVe vectors of the split sentences with
np.mean and prints the cosine, 1.0000, and "identical: True" — identical to
floating-point precision.

Word order is Chapter 6 (Language Models) and Chapter 7 (Transformers and
Attention).
:::

## Cosine measures relatedness, not similarity

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.roomy}
| pair                  | cosine    |
|:----------------------|----------:|
| `good` – `bad`        | 0.770     |
| `hot` – `cold`        | 0.725     |
| `increase` – `decrease` | **0.881** |
| `cat` – `dog`         | **0.880** |
| `cat` – `car`         | 0.311     |
| `teacher` – `student` | 0.808     |
:::
:::

::: {.column width="58%"}
- A pair of exact antonyms is *more* similar than two related animals
- Not a bug in GloVe: antonyms are perfectly substitutable — *sales increased sharply*, *sales decreased sharply* — so they keep identical company
- The embedding encodes *relatedness*; similarity and oppositeness are both kinds of it
:::

::::

::: {.takeaway}
[Never build a sentiment or polarity feature out of raw cosine between static word vectors.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
Static embeddings are useful, and weirder than the tutorials admit. Three defects
students should be able to name; this is the first.

This is the distributional hypothesis doing exactly what it promised.

A stronger version of the warning, not about static vectors at all: Steck,
Ekanadham and Kallus (2024) show that for a family of learned embedding models,
cosine similarity can be arbitrary — two regularisation choices that fit the data
equally well produce cosine values with no consistent relationship. Train the
objective you actually want to measure, or calibrate cosine against a baseline
from your own data, rather than treating 0.8 as meaning the same thing across two
models.

The benchmark community formalised the split with two datasets built on purpose:
WordSim-353 for relatedness (Finkelstein et al. 2002) and SimLex-999 for strict
similarity (Hill et al. 2015). Models score very differently on them — we see the
numbers shortly.
:::

## The space is not isotropic

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="46%"}
4,000 unit vectors from the top 50,000 GloVe words

::: {.roomy}
| statistic                     | value  |
|:------------------------------|-------:|
| mean cosine, random pairs     | 0.029  |
| standard deviation            | 0.119  |
| pairs with cosine > 0         | 56.9%  |
| norm of the mean vector       | 0.171  |
| mean cosine after centring    | −0.000 |
:::
:::

::: {.column width="54%" .compact}
- Isotropic null: mean cosine 0, variance $1/d$ — angles concentrate near 90°
- Mean cosine and mean-vector norm are one number: $(4000 \times 0.171^2 - 1)/3999 = 0.029$
- A shared component of measurable size: [tilted off centre, not crammed into a narrow cone]{.hl}
- Fix: subtract the mean, perhaps the top principal components too — one line (Mu & Viswanath 2018)
- BERT and GPT-2 are *more* anisotropic than static vectors (Ethayarajh 2019)
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
If embeddings used their space well, two random words would sit at a mean cosine
of zero. Be precise about the null, because the obvious phrasing is wrong: for
independent unit vectors drawn uniformly in d dimensions the angles do not spread
evenly; they concentrate near 90°, with mean cosine 0 and variance 1/d. Isotropy
means no direction is special, not that every angle is equally likely.

56.9% positive proves little on its own: the isotropic share would be 50%, and
the 8 million pairs come from 4,000 vectors, so they are nowhere near
independent observations.

The mean cosine and the mean-vector norm are not two pieces of evidence: for n
unit vectors, mean cosine = (n·‖mean‖² − 1)/(n − 1). Together they say there is
a shared directional component of measurable size, and removing it leaves a mean
cosine of zero. Centring does not make the covariance spherical, though.

The book's histogram widget: the raw distribution of cosines sits to the right of
zero; subtracting the mean vector recentres it. All-but-the-top improves most
similarity benchmarks for one line of code.
:::

## Frequency leaks in; your domain lives in the tail

::: {.lede}
Frequent words get more updates: mean norm 6.19 for the top 100 words, 3.62 for ranks 100,000–400,000.
:::

| term         | rank    | nearest neighbours                         |
|:-------------|--------:|:-------------------------------------------|
| `water`      | 430     | natural 0.70, dry 0.68, salt 0.68          |
| `turbine`    | 15,747  | turbines 0.80, compressor 0.78, generator 0.72 |
| `cavitation` | 109,044 | aliasing 0.56, barotrauma 0.54, attenuation 0.54 |
| `impeller`   | 124,835 | armature 0.62, evaporator 0.61, nozzle 0.60 |
| `eutectic`   | 159,022 | azeotrope 0.61, azeotropic 0.55, tiwai 0.54 |

::: {.takeaway}
Before shipping anything built on pretrained vectors, [read the neighbours of your twenty most important domain terms]{.hl}. If they look like `eutectic`, you need domain-adapted vectors, a subword model, or a different approach.
:::

::: {.notes}
Mean vector norm by frequency rank: 0–100: 6.19; 100–1,000: 5.85; 1,000–10,000:
5.45; 10,000–100,000: 4.99; 100,000–400,000: 3.62. Spearman(log rank, norm) over
the top 100k words: −0.313. Norm falls monotonically with rarity. Cosine ignores
norms, one more reason to prefer it — but any method using raw dot products,
Euclidean distance, or unnormalised embeddings as model input is partly modelling
word frequency.

More importantly, quality falls with rarity too. `turbine` at rank 15,747 is
excellent. `cavitation` returns `aliasing` and `attenuation` — plausible-sounding
technical words with nothing to do with pump physics. `eutectic` gets `azeotrope`
right, then breaks down into `tiwai` and `bifurcation`.

The chapter calls this the single most important practical point in the chapter
for engineers: pretrained embeddings are excellent for words Wikipedia discusses
often and unreliable for the vocabulary that defines your problem. It is much
cheaper to learn this now than after deployment.
:::

## Bias is in the data, and the geometry records it

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}
Projection onto `woman` − `man`

| word           | projection |
|:---------------|-----------:|
| `homemaker`    | +0.363     |
| `nurse`        | +0.329     |
| `receptionist` | +0.281     |
| `teacher`      | +0.152     |
| `doctor`       | +0.109     |
| `scientist`    | −0.046     |
| `programmer`   | −0.083     |
| `engineer`     | −0.123     |
:::

::: {.column width="60%" .compact}
Nobody put this in: it is a faithful measurement of how Wikipedia and news text used these words in 2014.

1. **A measurement, not a malfunction** — used deliberately, a quantitative instrument for studying bias in text
2. **It transfers to decisions** — a résumé screener inherits the association and applies it identically to every applicant, forever
3. **Debiasing is harder than it looks** — projected-out vectors [still cluster by gender]{.hl} (Gonen & Goldberg 2019)
:::

::::

::: {.src}
Bolukbasi et al. 2016 · Caliskan et al. 2017 · Gonen & Goldberg 2019
:::

::: {.notes}
The chapter lists the words in a different order (doctor, nurse, engineer,
teacher, programmer, homemaker, scientist, receptionist); the slide sorts them by
projection. Positive means the `woman` side.

The projection method is Bolukbasi et al.'s (2016), though they defined the gender
direction from the principal component of about ten word pairs rather than one
pair, which makes their axis less noisy and ours easier to check by hand.
Caliskan, Bryson and Narayanan (2017) showed embeddings reproduce the full range
of documented human implicit associations, including racial ones, with effect
sizes matching psychological studies.

Interviewers ask about all three consequences. On debiasing: the original method
projects out a gender direction. Gonen and Goldberg showed this mostly hides the
bias — a classifier recovers the original grouping with high accuracy. The
information was redistributed, not removed.

Ask the room the chapter's intuition check: is a model that shows no bias on
this test unbiased? No. The test measures one direction defined by one word pair;
bias not aligned with woman − man is invisible to it, and Gonen and Goldberg
demonstrated exactly that for debiased vectors — they pass the projection test
and fail a clustering test on the same data. Passing a fairness metric is
evidence about the metric, not the model. Report which test you ran, what it can
detect, and what it structurally cannot.
:::

## How do you know an embedding is any good?

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="52%" .compact}
- **Intrinsic**: does the space match human judgements — similarity ratings, analogies? Fast, no downstream task
- **Extrinsic**: does it improve the thing you care about? Slow, and [the only one that pays]{.hl}
- Same GloVe vectors, two benchmarks that disagree on purpose: WordSim-353 (relatedness) Spearman **0.533**; SimLex-999 (strict similarity) **0.296**
- Use intrinsic scores to catch gross breakage, never to choose between two reasonable candidates (Schnabel et al. 2015)
:::

::: {.column width="48%"}
Google analogies: **0.633** overall

| category                  | accuracy |
|:--------------------------|---------:|
| capital-common-countries  | 0.939    |
| capital-world             | 0.890    |
| nationality-adjective     | 0.879    |
| family                    | 0.816    |
| city-in-state             | 0.308    |
| opposite                  | 0.202    |
| currency                  | 0.152    |
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
The distinction matters in interviews.

The WordSim/SimLex gap is the headline: it is the quantitative version of
`increase`/`decrease` scoring 0.881, and it is why an intrinsic score is only
interpretable once you know which of the two your task needs. Schnabel et al.
showed that intrinsic rankings frequently disagree with extrinsic ones.

The Google analogy set: 19,544 questions in 14 categories. The per-category
breakdown is where the score stops being one number. Capitals are 0.939 and 0.890
because text states which city is the capital of which country constantly. But
currency is 0.152 and opposites 0.202. The model is not reasoning about
relations; it reproduces the ones its corpus repeats often. The headline 0.633
averages categories from nearly solved to nearly chance, which is why a single
analogy number should never be used to rank two embeddings.

The rest of the categories: gram1-adjective-to-adverb 0.244, gram3-comparative
0.791, gram4-superlative 0.543, gram5-present-participle 0.695, gram7-past-tense
0.554, gram8-plural 0.720, gram9-plural-verbs 0.584. Category names on the slide
drop the "gram6-"/"gram2-" prefixes.

A gensim detail: evaluate_word_pairs and evaluate_word_analogies default to
restrict_vocab = 300,000, so the 100,000 rarest GloVe vectors are never allowed to
be wrong — quietly flattering, given what we saw about the tail.
:::

## A comparison that looks better than it is

|                    | GloVe · 6 billion tokens | from scratch · 6.8 million tokens |
|:-------------------|:-------------------------|:----------------------------------|
| WordSim-353        | 0.533 · 0.0% skipped     | **0.627** · 11.9% skipped          |
| SimLex-999         | 0.296 · 0.1% skipped     | 0.268 · 13.4% skipped              |
| Google analogies   | 0.633                    | 0.200                              |

- The NumPy vectors "beat" GloVe on WordSim-353 — scored on the easy 88% of pairs. The skipped pairs are the rare ones, which are the hard ones
- Analogies do not escape it: the default skips questions with unknown words. GloVe already loses 58 (19,544 in the file, 19,486 scored)

::: {.takeaway}
[A model that refuses to answer looks more accurate than one that answers and is sometimes wrong.]{.hl} Always report coverage next to the score.
:::

::: {.notes}
Do not believe the 0.627. The from-scratch vocabulary is 18,677 words, so 11.9%
of benchmark pairs are skipped as out-of-vocabulary. GloVe is scored on all 353
pairs; the NumPy model on the easy 88%.

This is the most common way embedding comparisons are quietly wrong.

Including here: it would be convenient to say the analogy numbers, 0.200 against
0.633, escape the problem because both models face the same questions. They do
not. evaluate_word_analogies defaults to dummy4unknown=False, which skips any
question containing a word the model does not have. A model with an
18,677-word vocabulary loses far more questions, and the hard ones, so the two
scores do not share a denominator. To compare properly, score both with
dummy4unknown=True, which forces every model to answer all 19,544 questions and
counts a miss as wrong. Until that is run, quote each number with the count of
questions actually scored — which is what the book asks of everyone else.
:::

## Choosing between them

| method         | reach for it when                                               | watch out for                                                    |
|:---------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------|
| **PPMI + SVD** | the corpus is small, the vocabulary modest, and you must explain every number | the $V \times V$ matrix; no OOV handling; awkward to update |
| **word2vec**   | a large domain corpus in a language without heavy morphology    | OOV words raise an error; sensitive to hyperparameters           |
| **GloVe**      | you want good English vectors now, with no reason to train      | builds the co-occurrence matrix first; the same OOV failure      |
| **fastText**   | Turkish, Finnish, Hungarian, Arabic; unreliable spelling        | slower and larger; `kitap`/`kitle` at 0.667; weakest on short words |

::: {.small-note}
Better OOV coverage is not task accuracy: whether it converts is a separate measurement, and Ch. 4 found it did not on one. For documents, embeddings did not beat counting at classification; they win at similarity and retrieval.
:::

::: {.notes}
Four methods, all producing a dense vector per word, all comparable by cosine.
The differences only matter in specific circumstances.

Strengths, from the chapter's table. PPMI + SVD: no training loop; deterministic;
every step inspectable; works on small corpora. word2vec: streams over the corpus
(the model is still two V × d tables); fast, well understood, implementations
everywhere; skip-gram strong on rare words. GloVe: trained on the global matrix,
so it sees corpus-wide statistics; pretrained vectors excellent and free.
fastText: any word gets a vector, including one invented five seconds ago;
typo-tolerant.

Counting versus predicting as engineering, from the chapter. Memory: counting
holds a V × V matrix — 160 billion cells at V = 400,000 if stored densely, but
nobody does; the real cost is one monolithic artifact, expensive to build and to
update. Predicting streams, with memory V × d regardless of corpus size. Corpus
size: counting is comfortable on small corpora; predicting needs a lot of text
before gradient noise averages out. Determinism: counting gives the same output
for an exact solver (randomized SVD needs a seed; singular vectors are only
determined up to sign); predicting runs differ. New data: recount and
refactorize, versus keep training. The row that decides it in practice is new
data: counting is the better pedagogy and the better choice for a modest corpus;
predicting survives contact with a corpus that keeps growing.

Documents: averaged word vectors need no training and work instantly on unseen
documents, but destroy word order and negation. doc2vec scored 0.839 against
0.820 — about two standard errors on one split, a direction rather than a
verdict — and a new document needs gradient steps at query time. English
newsgroup posts are the easiest possible case for a bag of words; Chapter 4 (A
Representation Bake-Off) runs the comparison properly — a different language and
domain, seventeen times more data, and a learning curve that finds where the
ordering flips. Treat "embeddings did not beat counting" as a hypothesis until
then.
:::

## Where this is actually deployed {.smaller}

- **Airbnb search ranking** — listing embeddings from skip-gram on click sessions: session = sentence, listing = word, the booked listing as global context (Grbovic & Cheng 2018)
- **YouTube recommendations** — video and search-token embeddings averaged into a user vector, fed to a deep candidate generator (Covington et al. 2016)
- **Item2vec** — the same objective on purchase baskets and playlists; any `*2vec` is this pattern (Barkan & Koenigstein 2016)
- **fastText classification** — a linear model over averaged subword n-grams, trains in minutes on a CPU (Joulin et al. 2017)
- **Retrieval, everywhere** — every vector database and RAG pipeline (Ch. 20) runs this idea, with contextual vectors instead of static ones

::: {.takeaway}
[Embeddings are how you make discrete things differentiable.]{.hl} That is why the idea outlived the specific models.
:::

::: {.notes}
Static embeddings are not a historical curiosity. The technique — learn a dense
vector for a discrete item from co-occurrence, then do arithmetic on it — became
infrastructure far beyond text.

Airbnb: deployed to production search and reported as a substantial booking
gain. YouTube: the paper is the canonical description of two-stage
recommendation. fastText for classification: "on par with deep learning
classifiers" while training in minutes on a CPU — still an excellent first
baseline, and a good production answer for high-volume, low-latency text
routing. Retrieval: text as coordinates, compared by cosine — Chapter 20
(Retrieval-Augmented Generation).
:::

## What static embeddings cannot do {.smaller}

| limitation                   | evidence from this chapter                          | fixed by                        |
|:-------------------------|:---------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------|
| One vector per word form     | `python` blends Monty, PHP and the snake            | contextual embeddings (Ch. 7)   |
| No word order                | *pump failed / valve fine* = its reverse            | sequence models (Ch. 6)         |
| Out-of-vocabulary words      | word2vec `KeyError`; 7.3% of Turkish tokens         | subwords (fastText, BPE)        |
| Antonyms look like synonyms  | `increase`/`decrease` at 0.881                      | task-supervised fine-tuning     |
| Anisotropic geometry         | mean cosine 0.029 against 0 under isotropy          | mean removal, whitening         |
| Rare words collapse          | `eutectic` → `tiwai`                                | domain adaptation, subwords     |
| Bias from the corpus         | `homemaker` +0.363 on the woman axis                | no clean fix: measure, document |

::: {.takeaway}
A static embedding is a lookup table: one output per input. [To give `bank` a different vector by a river than in a market, compute it from the sentence.]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
Collecting the failures we accumulated, because together they are the
specification for the next part of the book.

The first two are the important ones, and they have the same root cause: a
static embedding is a function from word form to vector, and a function has one
output per input. The representation has to be computed from the sentence rather
than looked up — which is what Chapter 7 does, and why an LLM's contextual
vectors are computed from the sentence each time rather than stored per word.

The anisotropy row in full: mean cosine 0.029 against 0 under an isotropic null,
from a mean vector of norm 0.171; centring removes it.

The transition was not instant. ELMo (Peters et al. 2018) made it concrete by
running a bidirectional language model over the sentence and using its internal
states as the word representation — the moment "one vector per word" stopped
being the default. Everything after it, including every model in the book from
Chapter 7 onward, is a refinement of that move.
:::

## Intuition check 1 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
Your embedding has 300 dimensions. Why 300 and not 30 or 3,000?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Nothing magic: a bias–variance trade-off that bottoms out in the low hundreds for word-level tasks
- Too few, and unrelated words share coordinates — the 2-D toy space made almost everything similar
- Too many, and rare words get vectors fitted to a handful of contexts; memory and search grow linearly
- GloVe 50 → 100 dimensions: WordSim 0.503 → 0.533, SimLex 0.263 → 0.296, analogies 0.464 → 0.633
- [Tune it on the downstream task]{.hl}; past a few hundred, storage and latency decide
:::

::: {.notes}
Give students a minute before revealing (one click).

The published sweeps in Pennington et al. (2014) show the gains flattening beyond
roughly 300, which is why 300 became the default. The interview answer: tune it on
the downstream task, and past a few hundred dimensions the decision is usually
made on storage and latency rather than accuracy.
:::

## Intuition check 2 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
Why negative sampling instead of a softmax over the vocabulary?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Cost: a full softmax is 400,000 dot products per pair, times tens of billions of pairs
- Negative sampling makes $K + 1$ binary decisions, $K$ typically 5 to 20 — the cost per pair no longer depends on vocabulary size
- Deeper: it changes the objective. You no longer estimate $P(c \mid w)$; you discriminate real pairs from noise
- Its optimum is shifted PMI (Levy & Goldberg 2014): [principled, not merely cheap]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
The alternative is hierarchical softmax, which keeps the probabilistic
interpretation at O(log V) and is now rarely used.
:::

## Intuition check 3 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
You have 50,000 support tickets in Turkish. word2vec or fastText?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- fastText — and the reason should be [a number, not "Turkish is agglutinative"]{.hl}
- At 1.46 million tokens: 138,578 forms, 50% hapax, 7.3% unseen held-out tokens. 50,000 tickets is a *smaller* corpus
- Word-level vectors would rest on one or two occurrences for most of the vocabulary, and fail outright on unseen inflections
- The counter-argument: subwords make `kitap` look like `kitle` — if fine distinctions between short words matter, measure both
- Tickets have typos, and subwords absorb those too
:::

::: {.notes}
Saying the counter-argument is what separates a good answer from a memorised one.
:::

## Intuition check 4 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
Two documents' averaged vectors have cosine 0.95. Are they about the same thing?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Probably — but with much less evidence than the number suggests
- **Anisotropy**: random *words* already average 0.029, and averaged documents sit far higher. High cosines are cheap
- **Word order**: averaging destroys it, so opposite claims can average identically
- **Rare terms**: out-of-vocabulary and rare words — the discriminative ones — are dropped or badly estimated
- [Calibrate]{.hl}: report the percentile among random document pairs from your own corpus
:::

::: {.notes}
For averaged documents the floor is far higher than for words, because averaging
amplifies the shared component.

The professional move: compute the cosine distribution over random document pairs
from your own corpus and report the percentile rather than the raw number.
:::

## Intuition check 5 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
Should you fine-tune pretrained embeddings on your own corpus, or train from scratch?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- It depends on your corpus size relative to the pretrained corpus, and on how far your domain drifts
- Under ~10 million tokens: use pretrained vectors and do not update them
- 10 million to a few hundred million: initialise from pretrained and continue training
- Beyond that, or a vocabulary barely overlapping general text (chemical names, part numbers, clinical codes): from scratch
- [The diagnostic that beats all three]{.hl}: are your twenty key terms `turbine`-quality or `eutectic`-quality?
:::

::: {.notes}
Under ten million tokens, updating pretrained vectors only overfits the handful of
words you have.

These are rules of thumb from the chapter; the diagnostic is the part to
remember.
:::

## Intuition check 6 of 6 {.question}

::: {.ask}
"Embeddings replaced TF-IDF." True or false?
:::

::: {.fragment}
- False as stated: on 20 Newsgroups TF-IDF scored 0.853, and every dense method scored lower
- Sparse lexical retrieval (BM25) remains a strong baseline; production systems run lexical and dense retrieval together and fuse the rankings
- They fail differently: lexical matching is exact and handles rare identifiers, dense matching handles paraphrase
- [Embeddings replaced the *one-hot word*, not the TF-IDF *document*]{.hl}
:::

::: {.notes}
That distinction is worth stating explicitly, because it is usually the point of
the question.
:::

## Interview-style questions for discussion

::: {.lede}
Three of the chapter's twelve: one on the objective, one on the geometry, one on depth.
:::

1. Explain word2vec to someone who knows regression but not neural networks.
2. Two unrelated words have cosine 0.3. Is that high or low?
3. You have 100,000 items and click logs. Design an item embedding.

::: {.src}
Questions that recur in Huyen 2021 and the *Machine Learning Interviews* repository
:::

::: {.notes}
The chapter's caution on attribution: pages claiming to list "embedding questions
asked at Google" are search-engine content with no evidence behind them. These
questions recur across two credible free sources: Chip Huyen's Introduction to
Machine Learning Interviews and the Machine Learning Interviews repository on
GitHub.

The other questions in the chapter, for homework: skip-gram vs CBOW and when to
prefer each; why the 0.75 exponent; why subsampling improves the vectors rather
than just speeding things up; what is wrong with the king − man + woman demo; why
semantic search returns antonyms and what to do; document vectors for 50 million
documents under 100 ms; own-corpus embeddings worse than pretrained; detecting a
stale production embedding; the connection between PPMI+SVD, word2vec and GloVe.

Suggested format: pairs, one question each, two minutes, then the next slide.
:::

## What a strong answer names

::: {.compact}
1. **A logistic regression on word pairs** — $\sigma(v \cdot u)$, `score - labels` as the residual, a hidden layer with no activation. Then the caveat: both vectors are learned, so the loss is not jointly convex. Then Levy & Goldberg's shifted PMI — and that at low rank the two routes optimise different losses
2. **A baseline** — random GloVe pairs average 0.029 with standard deviation 0.119, so 0.3 is about 2.3 SDs above: high. But quote your own model's baseline, and note that centring removes the shared component
3. **word2vec on sessions** — session = sentence, item = word. Airbnb's refinements: the booked listing as global context, negatives from the same market (Grbovic & Cheng 2018). Then cold start: new items have no clicks
:::

::: {.notes}
Fuller answers from the chapter.

1. If they push back with "but isn't this a neural network?": yes, a shallow one,
   and the two are names for the same thing. An ordinary logistic regression fits
   weights over fixed features; this fits both vectors at once, so the score is
   bilinear and the optimisation problem is not the same even though the
   per-example arithmetic is. The qualifier about low rank separates someone who
   read the paper from someone who read the tweet.
2. Unanswerable without a baseline — that is the point of the question. The
   distribution is corpus- and model-specific. Mention anisotropy: the mean is
   0.029 rather than 0 (Mu & Viswanath 2018 for centring).
3. Negatives from the same market mean the model learns within-market
   distinctions. For cold start, propose content features or subword-style
   composition.
:::

## Exercises

:::: {.columns .compact}

::: {.column width="50%"}
1. **Redo the toy space** with window 1 and window 4. Why is a wider window more *topical*, a narrow one more *syntactic*?
2. **Break the analogy**: three that work, three that fail. Missing knowledge, or the wrong tool?
3. **Audit your own domain**: twenty terms, their GloVe rank and five neighbours, graded good / plausible / nonsense
4. **The Turkish vocabulary bill**: how many Turkish tokens to reach English's OOV rate?
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
5. **Make averaging fail on purpose**: two sentences from your field, opposite meaning, cosine above 0.99
6. **Beat TF-IDF** — tune doc2vec, 300-d vectors, Arora et al. 2017 — and check a different split
7. **Implement it**: CS224N Assignment 2, or add CBOW to the NumPy code and compare on rare words
8. **Measure a bias axis you care about**, then Gonen & Goldberg's clustering test
:::

::::

::: {.notes}
The chapter's eight exercises, shortened. Details worth reading out:

3. Report the correlation between rank and your grade. This is the exercise that
   most changes how people use pretrained vectors.
4. Take a Turkish corpus you own and an English one of similar size; reproduce the
   type/token and hapax numbers first.
5. Then write the design-review paragraph explaining why this representation must
   not gate that decision.
6. Options: tune doc2vec hyperparameters, use 300-dimensional vectors, apply
   Arora et al.'s weighted average with the first principal component removed, or
   concatenate more representations. Report what worked, by how much, and whether
   the gain survives a different train/test split.
7. Predict the direction of the CBOW vs skip-gram difference before you run it.
8. Pick a word pair defining an axis relevant to your domain, project twenty
   related terms onto it, report the ranking; after projecting the axis out, can a
   clustering still recover the original groups?
:::

## Where to go deeper

| source | why |
|:----------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|
| [Mikolov et al. 2013a](https://arxiv.org/abs/1301.3781), [2013b](https://arxiv.org/abs/1310.4546) | skip-gram and CBOW; then negative sampling — read the second twice |
| [Rong 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1411.2738) · [Goldberg & Levy 2014](https://arxiv.org/abs/1402.3722) | every gradient by hand; the negative-sampling objective in four pages |
| [Levy & Goldberg 2014](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/5477-neural-word-embedding-as-implicit-matrix-factorization) · [Levy et al. 2015](https://aclanthology.org/Q15-1016/) | the two papers that explained word2vec |
| [Bolukbasi et al. 2016](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.06520), then [Gonen & Goldberg 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1903.03862) | read as a pair: the fix, then the correction |
| [Jurafsky & Martin, Ch. 5](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/5.pdf) | PPMI, SVD, skip-gram and evaluation, with care; free |
| [Stanford CS224N](https://web.stanford.edu/class/cs224n/), lectures 1–2 | the skip-gram gradient; Assignment 2 implements word2vec |
| [Elena Voita, NLP Course For You](https://lena-voita.github.io/nlp_course/word_embeddings.html) | the best visual explanation of skip-gram and negative sampling |
| [fastText pretrained vectors](https://fasttext.cc/docs/en/crawl-vectors.html) | 157 languages including Turkish; start here |

::: {.notes}
From the chapter's list.

Papers, in reading order, all free: Mikolov et al. "Efficient Estimation of Word
Representations in Vector Space" then "Distributed Representations of Words and
Phrases"; Xin Rong's "word2vec Parameter Learning Explained" — the paper to read
if the original felt like it skipped steps, and the best preparation for
implementing it — paired with Goldberg and Levy's "word2vec Explained"; Levy and
Goldberg's "Neural Word Embedding as Implicit Matrix Factorization" and Levy,
Goldberg and Dagan's "Improving Distributional Similarity with Lessons Learned",
the second being the better model of how to do empirical NLP honestly; GloVe
(Pennington et al. 2014) and "Enriching Word Vectors with Subword Information"
(Bojanowski et al. 2017); Bolukbasi et al. then "Lipstick on a Pig" — a good
lesson in how fixes get overclaimed.

Watch: CS224N Lecture 1, word2vec derived at the board; Google's "Visualizing
High-Dimensional Space", four minutes that repair the intuition for "close in
embedding space".

Hands on: gensim and its word2vec tutorial, the fastest route to a model on your
own text; Jay Alammar's "The Illustrated Word2vec" (pictures) and Sebastian
Ruder's "On Word Embeddings" (the historical map); TensorFlow Projector, which
loads word2vec and GloVe in the browser with PCA, t-SNE and UMAP — look up your
own domain terms.

fastText pretrained vectors (Mikolov et al. 2018): trained on Common Crawl and Wikipedia.
:::
